title: How to never have to buy a training program again in your life
summary: NH lays out the chronological path to self-coaching: follow a varied novice program while building a list of lifts you know, start writing your own program once you want to, test it on paper and in the gym, then keep it as stable as possible with small spaced-out tweaks. When a program saturates, carry over what worked and build a new one.
claims: You should learn to coach yourself: you will lift for decades, and the knowledge gained is worth more than the money spent on coaches
Novices should not write their own programs; their programs are almost always bad because experience in the gym can't be replaced by papers or videos
Novice programs that only spam compound lifts are powerlifting-centric and neglect important movement patterns and muscle groups
The novice phase should be a phase of discovery with many movement patterns, so you aren't lost when an intermediate program brings more volume, variations and rep ranges
Don't rush novice gains; you won't make linear gains for 10 years, so adding 200 lb to your squat in six months is pointless
Almost everyone looks completely different after 6-12 months of training because muscles react strongly to the first stimulus
As a novice, keep a lifting variation list of every lift you have practised, ranked by how much you've done it; this is your data bank for programming
The lifts are the skeleton of a program; volume, intensity and frequency are built around them, not the other way round
NH defines the end of the novice phase as the moment you want to write your own program and stray from novice templates
NH started alone without knowledge and has followed his own programs from day one, which he admits was not optimal
Staying a novice for one or two years, twice as long as most, doesn't matter; what matters is staying in the game
Before running a new program, run an alpha test on paper and a beta test in the gym to catch problems
The best program is one that doesn't need to be changed every two weeks; constant program-hopping means you are relearning lifts rather than growing
Tweaks should be minimal and spaced out; small changes like moving a lift from 6-10 to 6-12 reps can happen more often, but replacing a lift should be rare
Having to swap a lift out means you didn't do your homework when building your lift list
A self-written program can run with minor tweaks for two to three years until it either works indefinitely or becomes too saturated
When a program stops working, transfer what worked (lifts, references, supersets) to a new program and discard the rest
Keep a separate list of lifts you want to try; introduce new lifts very lightly and accept a tuning phase of up to six months
With the right program and enough variations, one day can be done many different ways while repeating the same movement patterns, preserving specificity
We have a limited prime, so don't waste years on lifts that aren't optimal for you
